key_concept: Chromoplasts are coloured, non-photosynthetic plastids that contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments such as carotene and xanthophyll, which give plant parts their yellow, orange or red colour.
steps: Recall the classification of plastids by pigment content: chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll along with carotenoids. Their xanthophyll acts as an accessory photosynthetic pigment and is not stored.
Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments, carotene and xanthophyll. These colour fruits and flowers, for example ripe tomato and petals, so xanthophyll is stored here.
Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids. Amyloplasts store starch, elaioplasts store oils and fats, and aleuroplasts store proteins.
Aleuroplast and amyloplast are leucoplasts and carry no pigment, so they cannot store xanthophyll.
Therefore the plastid that stores xanthophyll is the chromoplast.
why_not_others: Chloroplasts do contain xanthophyll, but only as an accessory pigment for photosynthesis, not as a stored pigment. Aleuroplasts (proteins) and amyloplasts (starch) are colourless leucoplasts with no pigment at all.
common_trap: Students pick chloroplast because it also contains carotenoids, missing that the question asks for the plastid that stores the pigment.
time_saving_tip: Coloured but not green (carotene/xanthophyll) means chromoplast; any '-plast' that stores food (starch, oil, protein) is a colourless leucoplast and can be eliminated at once.
